Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/EPA View image in fullscreen An Ebola treatment centre in Rwampara, Ituri, DRC, 20 June 2026. There have been 3,360 confirmed cases of the virus in the east of the country. Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/EPA Global development Ebola outbreak in DRC the fastest growing in the history of the virus As the death toll rises to almost 1,500, and with a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain potentially still months away, health workers face a battle to slow the outbreak Supported by About this content Prosper Heri Ngorora in Bunia Fri 31 Jul 2026 04.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 04.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The latest numbers of confirmed cases of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has made this latest outbreak the fastest growing in the known history of the virus. At 3,360 confirmed cases , the disease is now affecting people in five provinces in the east of the DRC, with 1,487 deaths recorded, representing an overall case fatality rate estimated at about 45%, according to Congolese health officials. Health responses to the outbreak have been badly hampered by conflict in many of the affected areas. “I fear that at some point, life may come to a standstill here in our province of Ituri,” said Deborah Nzuva, a mother of four who lives in Rwampara, one of the affected regions. “We were already in a precarious situation before the Ebola virus disease, which continues to claim its victims.” Since officially declared by the Congolese authorities on 15 May, the Bundibugyo strain of the virus has spread faster than any of the country’s 16 previous Ebola outbreaks – and the numbers are approaching the previous worst toll, in 2018-2020 when 3,470 people in DRC were infected. Prof Pierre Akilimali, from the country’s public health institute (NPHI), is in charge of the Ebola response. He emphasises that the disease continues to spread and that it is still difficult to know when it will reach its peak. According to him, there is a way to go and the road to bringing the outbreak under control is a long one. View image in fullscreen Members of a Congolese Red Cross team in Bunia carry the body of a woman suspected of having died from Ebola, 7 June. Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty Images “Here in Ituri, we have the issues of insecurity, mining and high population density, which make the current outbreak more complex than previous ones,” he said. The Congolese authorities say they have taken a number of measures to limit spread, including strengthening surveillance through community liaison officers, building more than 20 Ebola treatment centres, and setting up local laboratories for testing. “The public must also play their part by seeking medical advice at the slightest suspicion of infection,” Akilimali said. “This will help us to respond effectively to the disease.” He said cases continue to rise in the Bunia and Rwampara health zones, with between 100 and 150 new confirmed infections each week. Annabelle Nissi, a clothing trader in Bunia, said people were living in fear. “This outbreak is causing us great distress. Our hope lies solely in God’s hands. It continues to disrupt our lives and has brought our development projects to a standstill,” she said. Dr Justus Nsio, field incident manager for the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said it was a race against time. First patients enrolled in record-breaking Ebola treatment trial in DRC Read more “All the experts monitoring this outbreak agree that it was detected too late. When detection is delayed, we have to work hard to make up for what we missed earlier in order to contain the disease,” he said. “What is certain is that, with the commitment of the movement and our partners, the outcome will be favourable.” View image in fullscreen Health workers prepare for a safe burial operation in the community of Mongbwalu, Ituri, DRC, in May. Photograph: Michel Lunanga/Getty Images Clinical trials began in early July of a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no standard treatment. As of 15 July, about 20 people had been enrolled in these trials, which could last up to four months, according to Prof Placide Mbala, head of laboratory operations for the Ebola response in the DRC. Uganda, which this week declared the Ebola outbreak over on its territory, 12 days after its last case was reported, has sent experts to the DRC to work alongside their Congolese counterparts, particularly in the border regions of Tchomia and Kasenyi. Beállítom Nem sokkal indítás után felrobbant a Kínai Népköztársaság egyik Hosszú Menetelés 7A hordozórakétája hétfőn délután – írja a South China Morning Post . A 60 méter hosszú, eddig kifejezetten sikeres rakétát a Vencsang Űrközpontból indították volna útnak, rakománya egy telekommunikációs műhold volt, amit a kínai űrügynökség geostacionárius pályára szándékozott állítani. Mind a rakétával, mind a műholddal elvesztették a kapcsolatot 90 másodperccel a kilövés után, a törmelék valószínűleg a Dél-Kínai-tengerbe zuhant. A ChinaSat-4B műhold ráadásul a Kínában eddig épített legdrágább műholdtípusba tartozik, egy ilyen műhold nagyjából 1 milliárd jüant, azaz majd 47 milliárd forintot ér. Hogy pontosan mi történt, azt egyelőre nem tudni, a kínai állami hírügynökség három órával az eset után annyit közölt, hogy „repülési anomália” áll a baleset hátterében. Szemtanúk szerint az úgynevezett Max Q pont környékén megroppanhatott a rakéta felső része. A Max Q azt a pontot jelöli, amikor egy kilövés után a legnagyobb dinamikus nyomás nehezedik a rakétára. A Hosszú Menetelés 7A modellnek eddig csak egyetlen sikertelen repülése volt, 2020 márciusában. A hibát akkor a négy gyorsítórakétában fellépő nyomásvesztés okozta, ami a vártnál alacsonyabb sebességhez és repülési magassághoz vezetett, végül pedig a küldetés megszakítását eredményezte röviddel a második fokozat működésének megkezdése után – írja a Spacejunkie . https://www.thenational.scot/news/266840.text: Media Russia Vladimir Putin Politics Russia's last free newspaper Novaya Gazeta closes after 33 years Media Russia Vladimir Putin Politics By Hannah Emma Shedden Political Reporter Share 0 Comments Novaya Gazeta will soon close its doors. (Image: Igor Ivanko/ AFP via Getty Images) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. RUSSIA'S last free newspaper has been forced to close after more than 30 years, saying it can no longer continue operating in the face of relentless pressure from the Kremlin. Novaya Gazeta (Новая газета) announced the news on Friday saying the decision to close was not their own but that they had "been killed". The paper said: "We didn't die, they killed us – along with the constitution. One can only laugh at Article 29 of the constitution, 'censorship is prohibited'". READ MORE: Oil giant BP reports 'obscene' profits amid huge rise in energy costs Novaya Gazeta consistently sought to challenge those in power and offer a perspective that differed from the Kremlin's official line. But the newspaper operated in an extremely restrictive press environment for decades, with its offices repeatedly raided, its journalists harassed and attacked, and the authorities went to great lengths to censor its reporting and cut off sources of funding. Since the paper's founding, six of its journalists – Ignor Domnikov, Yury Shchekochikhin, Anna Politkovskaya , Anastasia Buburova, Stanislav Markelov and Natalie Estemirova – were assassinated in contract-style murders. “We didn’t die, they killed us — along with the Constitution. One can only laugh at Article 29 of the constitution: ‘Censorship is prohibited,’” Muratov said. https://t.co/Pnxbe92Cl5 — Novaya Gazeta Europe (@novayagazeta_en) October 30, 2026 In recent years, the space for independent journalism in Russia has shrunk dramatically, particularly since the Kremlin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Just two months after the invasion, Novaya Gazeta's editor-in-chief and Nobel Peace Prize laureate, Dmitry Muratov, was attacked on a train travelling from Moscow to Samara, where red paint laced with acetone was thrown at his face. A spokesperson for the newspaper said: "On November 9 we will turn out the lights in the building where we've lived for 30 years, turn off the servers and leave. The newspaper is no more. "The Russian authorities and Russian security services have forced our newsroom to end its work." Due to the threat of intimidation, imprisonment and violence, most independent Russian journalists and papers have been forced to leave the country. Many relocated to the city of Riga, in Latvia. READ MORE : Glasgow council condemns far-right stunt at Nelson Mandela statue Founded in 1993 following the collapse of the Soviet Union, Novaya Gazeta became one of Russia's most respected investigative newspapers. It was established with financial support from former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, who used part of his Nobel Peace Prize money to help launch the publication. Over the years, it uncovered widespread state corruption, severe human rights violations, government overreach, and the grim realities of Russia's military conflicts. The paper broke the story of the "Gay Purges", where gay and bisexual men were being rounded up, illegally detained, tortured, and murdered in secret prisons in Chechnya. One of its most prominent investigations was the exposure of the 2004 Beslan school siege, proving that Russian special forces used indiscriminate heavy weaponry and flamethrowers that caused the fire killing most of the children. Anna Politkovskaya was murdered in 2006. (Image: Novaya Gazeta/Epsilon/Getty Images) For exposing this and the government's pre-attack warnings, the paper's journalists faced severe retaliation, including the near-fatal poisoning of Anna Politkovskaya as she tried to fly in to mediate the crisis. Then, in 2006, Anna Politkovskaya was assassinated outside her apartment block in Moscow on Vladimir Putin's birthday. The violence did not stop there. In 2009, human rights investigator Natalia Estemirova, a close collaborator of Novaya Gazeta and one of the newspaper's most important sources, was abducted outside her home in Chechnya. READ MORE: Scottish independence, Palestine and the left's Russia blind spot Hours later, she was found shot dead in neighbouring Ingushetia. Now, the publication that survived assassinations, censorship and relentless state pressure has finally been silenced. Finishing their statement, the paper wrote: "The values of the newspaper founded by Mikhail Gorbachev will be needed again back home. "For now it's up to readers to look after them. Take care of yourselves." Media Russia Vladimir Putin Politics Share 0 Comments Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading...
